nameStory: Wild geranium gets its "geranium" name from the Greek word "geranos," meaning crane, because its seed pods look remarkably like a crane's long, pointed beak. Many people also call it "spotted geranium" for the delicate darker veins that pattern its pink petals like nature's own watercolor brushwork. The "wild" part distinguishes it from those colorful potted geraniums on your porch, which are actually from a completely different plant family!
description: Wild geranium is a woodland wildflower that brightens up shady forest floors with clusters of rose-pink, five-petaled blooms in late spring. This native perennial grows 1-2 feet tall with deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch. After flowering, it develops those distinctive long, beak-like seed pods that give the plant its "cranesbill" nickname. It's a charming woodland resident that forms nice patches over time through underground stems.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five rounded pink petals with darker pink veins running through them like delicate brush strokes. Flowers are about an inch across and nod slightly on their stems, with ten prominent stamens surrounding the center.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided into 5-7 finger-like segments, resembling an open hand. The leaves feel soft and slightly velvety, with a fresh, green scent when crushed. They're arranged alternately along the stem.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The real showstopper - long, pointed seed pods that look exactly like a crane's bill, about an inch long. When ripe, they explosively split and curl upward, flinging seeds several feet away with an audible 'pop.'

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose clumps 1-2 feet tall and wide, often growing in patches connected by underground rhizomes. Stems are somewhat hairy and feel sturdy but flexible when gently bent.

habitat: Look for wild geranium in rich, moist woodlands throughout New England, especially in deciduous and mixed forests with good leaf litter. It thrives in partial shade under maples, oaks, and birches, often growing alongside other spring wildflowers like trilliums and bloodroot. You'll commonly find it on gentle slopes and in woodland clearings where the soil stays consistently moist but well-drained.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge in early spring, followed by the showy pink flowers from late April through June. This is prime identification time when both flowers and fresh foliage are at their most distinctive.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, focus on those characteristic crane's-bill seed pods which develop through summer and provide excellent identification even when flowers are gone. Leaves remain green and lush.
seasonality.fall: Foliage turns golden-yellow to reddish-brown, and old seed pods may still be visible. The plant begins dying back to its underground rhizome for winter.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts disappear completely, leaving only dried stems and seed pod remnants. Look for last year's distinctive beak-shaped pods scattered on the forest floor as clues to where plants will return.

funFact: Wild geranium seeds are natural ballistic missiles - when the long seed pods dry out, they suddenly split and the five sections curl upward like tiny catapults, launching seeds up to 30 feet away with enough force that you can actually hear them hit nearby leaves!
confusionNotes: Don't confuse wild geranium with those colorful potted "geraniums" sold at garden centers - those are actually pelargoniums from South Africa and have completely different leaves and flowers. Wild geranium's deeply divided, hand-shaped leaves and delicate pink flowers with visible veins are dead giveaways that you've found the real woodland native.
contextualKnowledge: There's a major naming mix-up in the plant world: what most people call "geraniums" in flower shops are actually pelargoniums, while true geraniums like this wild species are often called "cranesbills." This confusion dates back centuries to when European botanists first encountered both plant groups. True geraniums are hardy perennials native to temperate regions, while pelargoniums are tender plants from warmer climates.
compareHints: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands. Herb Robert has much more finely divided, fern-like leaves and tiny bright pink flowers, while most other geraniums in our area have smaller flowers and different leaf shapes. The combination of large, hand-shaped leaves and inch-wide pink flowers with dark veins makes wild geranium the most distinctive member of the family in New England forests.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
